doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Arriving in New York in 1950, the print shop and therapy
summary: He goes to New York in January 1950, works a print shop, studies with Lennie Tristano, and sees a therapist.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So when did you arrive in New York, officially?

Well when I got out of the Army, I was here for like a three day pass in the Army and a quick visit once before out of high school. But I went back to Seattle and re-entered the University of Washington. And this time instead of living at home I moved in to be closer to the campus. A friend had a houseboat on Lake Union that was full of musicians, and I lived there. And I met a drummer there who had been out on the road with bands and came from Olympia, Washington, but he’d been living in New York and he knew the scene. And we became friends. I played with a band he put together there in Seattle for a couple of months. But then he was going with a girl piano player that had come through and gotten stranded in Seattle, an all-girl band. And first he got a job so that she could work with him there and that was when I was playing with him. But then she decided that she was ready to go home so he decided he was ready to go to New York to be with her. And he was talking to me one night and he says, “You know, man, if you want to be a musician, you’ve got to go to where the music is, you know, it’s the only way you’re going to learn it and it’s the only way you’re going to get into it. So why don’t you come to New York with me?” It sounded reasonable to me, so I think we had our bus tickets and about fifty bucks, something like that. We got on the Greyhound and came out here. And that was January of 1950. And I guess, well I ran out of my fifty dollars pretty fast, and I had picked up the printing trade a little bit while I was in high school. I hadn’t done it since I’d been in the Army, but I remembered enough of it to go downtown and apply for a job feeding a hand press. And I think the first agency I went to they asked me enough questions that reminded me enough of what the terms were that I was able to go to the second one and sound like a professional, and they got me a job up in the Bronx at a horrible little print shop where people screamed at each other constantly. I kind of liked that work but I was used to people being nice. I had learned it in the small town, where the printers were all genial and humorous, and these people were just like — Arghhhh! But they were paying me thirty dollars a week, and out of that thirty dollars I was splitting a room with a drummer on 83rd street or 86th street, in the 80s there someplace, taking a weekly lesson with Lennie Tristano out in Flushing, on the valve trombone, I had switched to valve trombone to get more into jazz. And I was seeing a therapist. I was interested in the writings of Wilhelm Reich in those days. And the thing to do was to go get yourself straightened out by a well known therapist. So actually the therapist I found was quite sympathetic and he got me, I didn’t even know why I was there. I couldn’t give him a particularly good reason. But he got me into a different place. I had always been a very nice boy who tried to please everyone, and felt very anxious because some people I couldn’t seem to please.
